concept.name: Nominal effective exchange rate
concept.definition: A trade-weighted index of a currency's nominal value against a basket of trading-partner currencies — in the BIS methodology, calculated as a geometric trade-weighted average of bilateral exchange rates. An increase in the NEER indicates a nominal appreciation of the currency; it is the building block from which the real effective exchange rate is derived by adjusting for relative prices.
concept.intuition: The NEER collapses a currency's many bilateral exchange rates into one number weighted by how much you trade with each partner.
concept.mechanics: Bilateral rates are combined as a weighted geometric mean using weights derived from manufacturing trade flows, double-weighted to capture direct bilateral trade and third-market competition; weights are time-varying on a three-year basis. BIS broad NEER indices cover 64 economies (narrow indices 26) and use published US dollar exchange rates as inputs where possible.
concept.formula: NEER_t = Product over i of S_i,t^(w_i), where S_i,t is the bilateral exchange-rate index against partner i and w_i are trade weights summing to 1 (geometric trade-weighted average).
concept.failure_modes: NEER ignores inflation differentials, so a country with high inflation can show a stable NEER while losing real competitiveness; results also depend on the weighting scheme and base period, limiting cross-provider comparability.
concept.misconceptions: The NEER is not a forecast or an equilibrium measure — it is a descriptive weighted average, and its level is meaningful only relative to the index base year.
concept.example: If the euro appreciates against the dollar and yen but weakens against sterling, the BIS euro NEER moves by the trade-weighted net of those changes rather than by any single pair.
